pattern: \bpermanent home is outside (?:of )?South Carolina\b[^.]{0,80}\bbuyer must (?:hold back|withhold)\b
struck: When the seller's permanent home is outside South Carolina, the buyer must hold back part of the sale for South Carolina income tax.
use: When the seller's permanent home is outside South Carolina, the buyer must hold back part of the price for South Carolina income tax, unless the sale is exempt.

struck: An LLC taxed as a partnership is withheld at the individual rate.
use: (cut it: no source names LLCs; the statute puts a nonresident partnership at the top individual rate and a corporation or other nonresident entity at 5 percent)

struck: An out-of-state LLC with no SC business history is a nonresident.
use: A business seller can be treated as a resident on the same form if it has done business in South Carolina for the last two tax years, will keep doing it, is registered here and has filed a South Carolina return with none overdue.

struck: Any real property in the United States is like-kind to any other: a condo for a house, land for a duplex.
use: Real property in the United States is generally like-kind to other US real property, improved or not, as long as both are held for business or investment: a rental condo for a rental house, land for a duplex.

pattern: \bis the safe harbor\b|\bthe only safe harbor\b
struck: A qualified intermediary holding it under a written agreement that limits your rights is the safe harbor.
use: A qualified intermediary holding the money under a written agreement that limits your right to it is one of the IRS safe harbors.

struck: Trading with a relative: if either of you sells the property you got within two years, the deferred gain is taxed.
use: Trading with a close family member (a spouse, parent, grandparent, child, grandchild, brother or sister) or a company you control: if either of you sells the property you got within two years, the deferred gain is taxed, with a few exceptions such as a death.

pattern: \bused it yourself no more than\b|\byour own use\b[^.]{0,40}\b(?:14 days|10 percent)\b
struck: In each of those two years you rented it at a fair rent for 14 days or more and used it yourself no more than 14 days or 10 percent of the rented days, whichever is more.
use: In each of those two years you rented it at a fair rent for 14 days or more, and personal use was no more than 14 days or 10 percent of the rented days, whichever is more. Days your family uses it, or anyone pays less than a fair rent, count as personal use.

struck: The IRS extends them only for presidentially declared disasters.
use: The IRS can postpone the 45 and 180 days after a federally declared disaster, but never past the tax return's due date with extensions.

struck: A company created by your qualified intermediary, called an exchange accommodation titleholder, parks the title.
use: Another party that is not you or your agent, called an exchange accommodation titleholder, takes title to the new property first.

struck: The agreement must be signed within 5 business days, and the 45-day and 180-day limits still apply.
use: You and the titleholder sign a written agreement within 5 business days after it takes title.

struck: Reverse exchanges cost more in intermediary fees, and financing is harder. Fewer lenders will do that.
use: (cut it: no source)

struck: A share of a Delaware statutory trust can be the replacement.
use: A share of a Delaware statutory trust can be the replacement if the trust stays inside the IRS ruling's limits and the other 1031 rules are met.

struck: When those owners sell, the buyer must withhold unless the seller's form says otherwise.
use: (cut the link: a tax-bill address is not a home state; state the withholding rule on its own, from row 1)

struck: Houses about $350,000 (middle half $266,000 to $500,000).
use: Houses and other homes that are not condos sold for about $350,000 in the middle (middle half $266,000 to $500,000).

pattern: \bholds? back\b[^.]{0,160}\bnothing with\b|\b(?:holds? back|withhold(?:s|ing)?|keeps? back) nothing\b|\bnothing (?:is )?(?:held back|withheld)\b
struck: At closing South Carolina holds back about $19,600 with no form, about $9,700 with the I-295 stating the gain, and nothing with the exchange box and a qualified intermediary.
use: With the exchange box and a qualified intermediary, the amount goes to the intermediary at closing, and the state is paid nothing if the exchange is completed.

struck: The seller can ask for a refund on Form I-290X.
use: Before the end of the tax year, the seller asks for the refund on an amended I-290; after it, on the South Carolina return.

struck: The withholding the intermediary holds can be used toward the replacement.
use: (cut it: the ruling does not say the intermediary's withholding amount may be spent on the replacement)
